rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says provision should reach people unable to acquire wealth through disability or limited means; voluntary spending advances spiritually, while those with sufficient wealth owe the poor's prescribed share to government.
rows.anchor: the greatest means for this spiritual advancement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the fay dispute's specific context, Muslims must take what the Prophet gives and abstain from what he forbids; the warning bars objections and calls them to fear God, stern in retribution.
rows.anchor: whatever the Prophet (sws) gives them should be taken and whatever he stops them from, should be abstained from

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing warning shows that hypocrites raised the preceding questions as objections from habit, not as sincere inquiries; sincere Muslims would not have needed this warning.
rows.anchor: the answers to the questions which have been given here had been raised by the hypocrites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though tied specifically to the preceding instructions, the command establishes general obedience to the Prophet in every matter as God's appointed guide; 4:64 confirms this, giving the passage both contextual and comprehensive sharīʿah meanings.
rows.anchor: the principle which can be derived from it is absolutely general

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage moves from the general spending category for fay to its most important specific need in those circumstances: helping immigrants who had fled their homes for Madīnah.
rows.anchor: helping the immigrants, who, at that time, were abandoning their homes and coming to Madīnah from all places

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The immigrants sought God's bounty through their faith and trust; that faith let them abandon homes and property without knowing where they could find shelter.
rows.anchor: vacated their houses and properties without even caring if they had any place to seek shelter in

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their aim in migrating was to remain beside the Prophet, ready to support and help God and His Messenger.
rows.anchor: the great objective for which they undertook this major step: they wanted to remain alongside the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The immigrants are called truthful in faith because they sacrificed everything for God's pleasure and to support His Prophet; hypocrites who claim faith but refuse even slight loss are liars, as 59:11 says.
rows.anchor: it is these people who are truthful in their claim to faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse praises the Anṣār and earliest Muhājirūn for welcoming later immigrants without resentment or envy over their share in wealth and fay, and for preferring them despite their own needs.
rows.anchor: they do not feel any resentment that the immigrants have come over to them in multitudes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The coordinated expression suppresses a verb suited to its second object; the omission is recoverable from contextual indications, as in the Arabic analogies cited.
rows.anchor: a verb which is appropriate for the second object is suppressed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As an example of the omitted verb, Islahi proposes ḥakkamū, yielding the sense that these people already had homes and had firmly rooted their faith.
rows.anchor: those who already have a place of residence and have also firmly rooted their faith

words: وَٱلَّذِينَ تَبَوَّءُو ٱلدَّارَ وَٱلْإِيمَٰنَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase primarily includes the Anṣār, but Islahi also includes the earliest Muhājirūn already settled in Madīnah with livelihoods: together they preceded later migrants in residence and faith, while the Anṣār alone preceded them only in having homes.
rows.anchor: both of them are collectively ahead of the later ones

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They affectionately welcomed the many new arrivals and accepted that fay wealth would go to them or be shared with them, contentedly placing the newcomers' needs first.
rows.anchor: they are giving preference to their needs over their own

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Praising their altruism teaches believers to show mutual sympathy and generosity, while implicitly shaming hypocrites who demanded that Banū Naḍīr's remaining wealth be distributed as war spoils.
rows.anchor: the believers should be sympathetic, generous and altruistic to each other

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuḥ means greed and avarice; as a craving of the soul it is dangerous, and failure to master it can ruin one's Hereafter. Islahi renders it “selfishness” to stress this danger.
rows.anchor: it becomes evident that it is one of the cravings found in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi warns that the hypocrites suffer from this spiritual disease and, unless they reform, will be doomed eternally.
rows.anchor: This section of verses tells the hypocrites that they are inflicted with this malady

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi cites a narration that selfish greed destroyed earlier nations by driving them to tyranny, sin and defiance, and severing kinship ties.
rows.anchor: It induced them to tyranny and they became tyrannical

rows.speaker: exegetes
rows.claim: The exegetes take the verse to add the Anṣār to the beneficiaries of fay, just as the preceding verses assign a share to the Muhājirūn.
rows.anchor: Our exegetes are of the opinion that just as the previous verses state that the Muhājirūn also have a share in the wealth of fay

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects that reading: the Muhājirūn were mentioned because their needs strained the government, whereas no one disputed the Anṣār's share, and the previously named poor already included needy Anṣār.
rows.anchor: I am unable to understand this

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse instead says that the Anṣār and early Muhājirūn did not view incoming brothers as a financial threat: they welcomed them affectionately and stood ready to sacrifice, exemplifying the mutual care faith requires of every Muslim.
rows.anchor: they, in fact, welcome them with affection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Later Muhājirūn are likewise sincere and affectionate toward earlier believers and migrants; though deprived of resources and homes, they do not envy them and pray for forgiveness and freedom from rancor.
rows.anchor: migrated before them. They are not envious of the fact that they have taken into possession all available means and resources

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer against malice hints that they fear Satan may provoke envy when they see earlier believers enjoying comfort they lack, and instead ask God to fill their hearts with love.
rows.anchor: once we see them in comfort and ease which we do not have

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier warning about selfishness contrasts with the truthful, righteous people, who are entirely free of that spiritual disease.
rows.anchor: in contrast, these truthful and righteous people are absolutely devoid of such maladies

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Banū Naḍīr's defeat, Islahi reconstructs hypocrites encouraging the remaining nearby Jewish tribe, Banū Qurayẓah, to resist, perhaps conspiring with them and promising aid in exile or war.
rows.anchor: After that they started to encourage and embolden the Banū Qurayẓah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an assures Muslims that hypocrites are cowards and liars who will not join exile or battle and would be routed if they fought; it warns Banū Qurayẓah they will share Banū Naḍīr's fate and be disowned like Satan in 59:16.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ān assured the Muslims that these hypocrites are absolute cowards and liars
